> 解。利西南；无所往，其來復吉；有攸往，夙吉。

Hexagram 40 is about loosening, and its character is one of the great pictures in the language.

## 解 is 從刀判牛角

說文: 解，判也。從刀，判牛角.

Knife, ox, horn: three things, one action — taking a blade to an ox's horn and opening it.

The original sense is not "to dissipate." It is to split open. From the beginning it is a hand, a force, and an object.

## 庖丁解牛

The most famous use of the character is in 莊子·養生主, and the cook says the thing that matters:

良庖歲更刀，割也；族庖月更刀，折也。今臣之刀十九年矣，所解數千牛矣，而刀刃若新發於硎.

A good cook changes his blade once a year, because he cuts. An ordinary cook changes it once a month, because he hacks. This blade is nineteen years old, has opened thousands of oxen, and is as sharp as it was coming off the whetstone.

Why? 以無厚入有間，恢恢乎其於游刃必有餘地矣 — because he puts what has no thickness into the gap, and the blade has room to move.

Not a sharp blade. A gap found between the joints.

Which is exactly 解's sense: not prying the knot loose, but finding the seam and following it with one stroke.

And it makes 動而免乎險 legible: the movement is along the seam, and that is why it escapes the danger instead of breaking the blade.

## 夙吉

夙: early. When things are loosening, act early. Do not let the knot re-tighten while the tension is down.

## 田獲三狐，得黃矢

九二: hunting and taking three foxes, and getting a yellow arrow.

Fox: what is hidden, what lurks. Clearing the hidden sources of trouble.

黃 is the colour of the centre; 矢 is the straight thing. Two characters, two virtues: 中 and 直.

## 負且乘

六三 負且乘，致寇至，貞吝.

Carrying a load on one's back, and riding in a great carriage.

The 繫辭上 gives Confucius's explanation: 負也者，小人之事也；乘也者，君子之器也。小人而乘君子之器，盜思奪之矣.

Carrying is the work of a subordinate; riding is the vehicle of a superior. A subordinate sitting in a superior's carriage, and the thief starts thinking about it.

So the line is not about showing off money. It is about a mismatch between standing and equipment: the thing being used does not belong to the position held, and the gap is what invites the theft.

## 解而拇

九四 解而拇，朋至斯孚.

拇: the big toe.

The character appears twice in the book — 咸初六 咸其拇, sensation starting at the toe; and here, 解而拇, loosening starting at the toe. Both begin at the lowest, most attached point.

So the release begins at the base: untie the foot first, and then companions arrive and trust follows.

## 射隼于高墉之上

上六 公用射隼于高墉之上，獲之，無不利.

隼: a hawk, perched on a high wall — fierce, exposed, hard to take.

高墉: the high wall, the position of power.

The top of the hexagram does not loosen anything. It takes aim and removes the conspicuous source of harm from where it sits, and only then is nothing unfavourable.

## 赦過宥罪

The 象: 君子以赦過宥罪 — pardon faults, be lenient with offences.

過 and 罪 are distinguished: the slip and the crime.

Which is the last instruction of the chapter and the most useful one: after a knot opens, the thing to do with what was held in it is to sort errors from offences, and to be generous with both.

## The test

Take a problem that has been tight for a long time. Ask whether you have been cutting or hacking — whether you are looking for the seam between the joints or applying more blade. The cook with the nineteen-year-old knife was not stronger.
